source: Make a 3D tower defense game where we see the game looking down into the map (so it appears 2D). The map, towers and enemies should be actual parts and not GUIs. There should be a round system where it goes up to round 50 and any more is "freestyle". We should have coins and a shop to buy more towers. We should have GUIs to start round, button to open shop, and we should drag and drop a tower to an allowed area. When we drag a tower, we see a radius showing its reach and the radius is red if we try to put it on a disallowed area such as the path

image_prompt.text: Flat placement zones framing both sides of the enemy path, visually distinct from the path so allowed and disallowed ground read at a glance from directly overhead
The structure at the end of the track that the waves are trying to reach
A narrowing in the lane where waves bunch up and area-damage towers pay off
Everything - map, towers and enemies - built as real parts, readable from a fixed overhead camera with no vertical complexity

layout_placement.text: The core at the end of the lane representing the player's health pool
The mouth of the track where each enemy wave enters

notes: The map must read correctly from a fixed top-down camera so the 3D scene appears 2D; keep elevation out of the lane and the build zones.
Allowed and disallowed placement ground is a hard layout property here, not just a visual - the drag-and-drop validity check reads it directly.
Round 50 is the boundary between the scripted wave ladder and endless freestyle mode; the map does not change at that point unless the user wants it to.

coverage_missing.ask: What should the map look like?
What ends a run - the core's health reaching zero, or something else? No core or lives were mentioned.
How large is the playable map in studs?
Single winding lane or multiple entrances?

answers.ask: No theme was stated - grassy toy-soldier board, sci-fi platform, or something else?
answers.answer: Use a grassy toy-soldier board theme, with a simple dirt path and clearly marked build areas.

answers.ask: How big should the map be, given it all has to fit in one overhead view?
answers.answer: Keep it small: one compact map that fits comfortably in a single overhead view, with room for the path and a modest number of towers.

answers.ask: One enemy lane, or several that converge on the core?
answers.answer: Use one enemy lane for a simple, clearly playable first map.
